utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. Before we start with the witness, the Chamber would like to return to the pending admission of certain numbers of pages of Momir Nikolic's interview with the Prosecution, which, after instruction by the Chamber on 12th of April, the Defence uploaded their 65 ter numbers 1D730 and 1D731 respectively. The Chamber grants admission of 65 ter numbers 1D730 and 1D731 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D730 shall be assigned Exhibit D220. 65 ter document 1D731 shall be assigned Exhibit D221. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. With respect to the pending admission of pages selected from 65 ter 1D211, a chapter of a book by Cees Wiebs, uploaded by the Defence as 1D735 and used with Witness Rupert Smith, the Chamber notes that on 28th of March, 2011, the Defence submitted it would seek to tender some 15 pages of this larger document. This selection of pages by the Defence, now uploaded as 1D735, in fact, amounts to 21 pages. Mr. Gajic, could you please explain this discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we reviewed the document. And taking out some of the pages would result in having the same amount in the end, if we tried to remove the left-hand side of the page and leave the right-hand side, and this would also result in a text that would be difficult to read. We believe that those additional five pages in e-court does not require much space or time to read. On the contrary, the text would be easily legible and the parties will have an opportunity to see what references were for the document and what were the starting points in order to analyse those parts that the Defence is interested in. It would simply be useful, we believe, to have the document uploaded in this integral shape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: With this explanation by the Defence, this document will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D735 shall be assigned Exhibit D222. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If there are no additional matters to be raised, then the witness should be brought in, please. In the meantime, I would like to ask Mr. Tolimir, and would like to invite him, to consider this way of examination of the witness: You know, the document you have quoted a lot yesterday, the regulations for the military police, are in evidence already. They were tendered by the Defence, they are a Defence exhibit, and we can use this. There is no need to quote it, lengthy, into the transcript, as have you done earlier with another witness. I think this is really a waste of time. You are, of course, entitled to put questions to the witness about the content and his knowledge about the content of this document, but there's no need to read and read and read again. We have it on this transcript, we have it in evidence, and, therefore, you should shorten your -- this kind of question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to invite both parties to speed up and to try to finish with Mr. Todorovic today. Please sit down. Good morning, Mr. Todorovic. Welcome back to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Gajic turn his microphone off, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, please turn off -- thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to greet everyone, and may these proceedings be concluded in keeping with God's will, not my own. And I'd like to wish the witness a pleasant stay in the courtroom. Mr. President, I had to go through the Rules of Service of security organs because Mr. Obradovic, who was the other witness through whom it was tendered, could only address the command part, and this witness could address the work of the security organs. The same applies to D202, which was also introduced through Ljubo Obradovic. He only addressed the command part, whereas this witness will speak to the work of security organs, by your leave. He mentioned yesterday that he had to co-ordinate his work with the regulations and rules that were in place. I would like to have D202 shown in e-court, which is the Rules of Service of the land forces in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, to avoid any misunderstanding, this was not the problem I raised. It is a time-consuming exercise to read all these articles and paragraphs of this document again into the transcript. You may put questions in that respect, of course. This is your right, and that is the purpose of the cross-examination. But please avoid time-consuming reading. The document is now on the screen. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see the regulations, Mr. Todorovic. I wanted to refer to page 3, general provisions. I will read from paragraph 2 of Article 1, what are the competencies --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness [sic] please wait for the English page to appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "According to the regulations, the definition of responsibilities shall comprise the rights, obligations, and scope of work of command organs and officers of these organs in the execution of the stipulated work and tasks." You, as a security organ in the East Bosnian Corps, did you only have the rights and obligations from the scope of work of security organs or did you also have certain duties to undertake regarding command or the issue of command?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had rights, duties, and obligations to perform tasks prescribed for the work of organs and departments of security and intelligence organs in the corps command. Occasionally, I was also included in the work of some other bodies in performance of different tasks, but these mainly entailed brief periods of time as a member of certain commissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Let us look at Article 4, paragraph 4, which clearly indicates the following -- that is, the last paragraph of Article 4. It's actually the third paragraph on this page. It reads --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think you didn't understand what I was telling you at the beginning. I think there's no need to read and read and read these articles into the transcript. The witness may have a look on it; and put a question to the witness what is -- about his interpretation of this article, about his knowledge, how it worked at the relevant time, but please avoid reading, reading, reading. It's really a time-consuming exercise. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This precisely has to do with what was discussed in examination-in-chief. It was alleged that I took over responsibilities of another organ. That is why I want to ask the witness this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Having in mind this paragraph 4, which I won't read, as instructed by the Judge, does a command organ have the right to assume responsibilities of a superior or a subordinate organ, or does it have the right to delegate some of its own powers to it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, no. In exceptional situations, a corps commander may authorise someone else to act on his behalf in the performance of certain tasks, but this has to be within a specified, short time-frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is this exception regulated by another rule?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is regulated by the Rules of Service in the armed forces, that is to say, in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at Article 6, paragraph 1, please, which confirms clearly what you said a number of times yesterday. Here we can see who has the exclusive right of command. Who has that right in the units of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exclusive right of command -- apologies. The exclusive right of command in JNA units, and later on VJ units and VRS units, is with the commanders in question. They are responsible for all their subordinates. They command their subordinate units as well as those units that were attached to them or used as reinforcements.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at page 6 in the English and 7 in the B/C/S version. These are special provisions; Article 9, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It states who commands and controls subordinate units and institutions?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, the right of command is an exclusive right of commanders to order commands to their subordinate commanders, which includes a clear implementation of tasks and orders. And in the JNA, the VJ, and the VRS, it was based on the principle of singleness of command and subordination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I believe you need the next page in B/C/S, because Mr. Tolimir asked for paragraph 2 of Article 9. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see Article 6. Actually, it is item 6 of this article. My question is: Who has the exclusive right of control of the Security Service in the VRS and the FRY, according to the regulations?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said a few times yesterday, security organs are managed by commanders in whose formations they are to be found, depending on whether it's at the level of administration, department, or else -- or something else. Specialist direction is provided by the security organ of the superior command.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 7 in the Serbian and 8 in the English version, please. It is item 10 of this article. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: Do all subordinate organs in the command of a corps or brigade have to be commanded by the commander, exclusively, or can they receive commands from some other organs as well?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander is responsible for the overall situation. As for the various departments, they are directed, controlled, and they propose measures to the commander, as well as further education, by the chiefs of arms and services.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do chiefs of arms and services have the right to manage or provide specialist assistance to the respective organs in keeping with commanders' instructions?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The organs of services control and direct the work in their sphere; specifically, the Security Service organ controls and directs the work of the organs of the military police. If there is a need to intervene because of a found situation, he proposes measures to the commander, and the commander then issues an order that these -- or that specific actions be executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 17 in the Serbian and page 14 in the English. This is Article 14, the general paragraph of this Article 14, and you can see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: The organs for the arms, do they have the same powers as the security organs at the corps commands? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they do. Just like the artillery chief is responsible for the artillery units within the corps command, in the same way the security chief is responsible and has duties vis-à-vis combat readiness of the military police units. He proposes, as I already said before, measures to improve, stimulate, equip those forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 8 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And my question, after you look at the text, is this: You spoke about that before. When the commander is absent, who then is in command of the brigade and the other subordinate corps units? We can see this item now. Actually, we can see what Article 10 says on page 10, I think it is. Okay, it's not -- we're not seeing it right now. Maybe you can switch. When the commander is absent, who is in command of the Security Service and the other units of the corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As opposed to the other units, the artillery, engineers, the ABHO, and so on, when the commander is absent, the only person, pursuant to the general issues of security, can be led by the deputy commander or his chief. He can also be represented for a short period of time by somebody else authorised to do so by the commander, and they can command the service only on general matters and not where the security and intelligence matters are concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at page 19 in the Serbian and page 16 in the English, and can we see what the responsibilities are of the organ for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You were the security and intelligence chief in your corps. Could you please tell us what the responsibilities were?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure whether it's the logistics or the security organ that the accused refers to here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please help us to clarify. What are you talking about? At the moment, we have Article 17 on the screen, "Organ for Intelligence Work," but you were referring to another. In your last question, you were asking about the organ for logistics. I don't see the link. The way we see it here on page 9, lines 20, "responsibilities ... of the organ for logistics." Perhaps it's a mistranslation. I have no idea. Please clarify that and repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question to you, Mr. Todorovic, is: Since at the same time you were the organ for intelligence and the organ for security, can you please tell us, what does the Intelligence and Reconnaissance Service at the command do?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to avoid reading, because the presiding Judge has already warned us about that and I think everyone has the text in front of them, it is precisely what it states in Article 17, without any need to add or take anything away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Can you please tell us if the intelligence organ has the right to command the reconnaissance units that are part of it or not?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does not have the right to command, but they can write orders for intelligence engagement, regulating the engagement of the reconnaissance units, and this order would then be signed or approved by the corps commander. They are monitoring or observing the work, and intervene in case that is required. Again, I emphasise: Command, in the first, second, and the third armies that I was a member of, is done according to the principle of singleness of command. There is one commander, and he makes all the decisions. His assistants propose things, and then he would entirely approve them, perhaps correct and then approve them, or not approve these proposals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Does that mean that the security organ only has the right to propose to the commander but does not have the right to use and command, in itself?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please look at 35 in Serbian and 35 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And now my question is this: The security organ, and that was what you were doing, can you please tell us what the function of the security organ is in the corps command? What is it in the corps command? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security organ in the corps command, as it states here, is a professional, specialised organ in order to organise and implement security measures, so I don't need to read further from the text. Its primary assignments are intelligence and counter-intelligence ones. And if needed, I can explain what the intelligence tasks are. Then it is engaged on general security measures and also the manner in which the military police and their units can be used in the best and the most effective way. And also it is responsible for matters of training and exercise. That would be that, in brief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Can we please look at pages 31 in Serbian and in the English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Since we have now seen what the professional organ, as you have emphasised here, does, can you please tell us, what does the security organ states in the command, as a professional organ?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're not looking at the correct page here. We need to look at Article 29, item 9. We're looking at Article 26. I'm sorry, I did not make the correct reference for the e-court. Can we ask the e-court to show in the Serbian, please, page 36. And now we see it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Item 9. My question is: The security organ in the command security organs, is it just a professional unit, a organ of the commander, or does it have any other powers or responsibilities? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other than its tasks and duties within the corps command, and I already referred to them a number of times, saying that it is responsible for the situation, in the professional sense, the situation in the military police unit, then it is responsible for professional direction and for providing assistance to the subordinate security organs in the member units as well as the units of the military police. That is that parallel line of professional direction and control of organs of the military police from the top down to the lowest units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. And along this specialist line, to whom is this person reporting to, to which person? The security organ, to whom does it report to for the specialist area of its work? Which superior does that organ report to along the specialist line?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The specialist management is subject to control by the superior security organ, meaning that it ultimately reports to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sir, this is the rules on the land forces operation in peacetime, so is that organ responsible to the commander or to the superior commander? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I fail to understand the essence. Thus, the security organ is responsible for its overall work to the commander, its commander in whose unit it is. As for this specialist directing or managing --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the end of your answer. It was not caught by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The security organ, specifically speaking about myself, the chief of the Sector for Intelligence and Security Affairs in the East Bosnia Command, I'm responsible for my specialist activities to the commander of the East Bosnian Corps. In my previous answer, I said that according to the specialist line I am responsible to the chief of the Sector for Intelligence and Security Command, but this is according to the specialist line, not according to the command-and-control line. So I made a slip of the tongue there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. In that case, I would like to ask to look at D203 once again in order to avoid any confusion, so that it can be understood that both you and I are trying to present the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at page 8 in the e-court, both in English and Serbian. Let's look at Article 12 of the document that we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you now referring to D203 or D202?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are now calling up 203. We can see it on the screen. We can see item 12 on our monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Sir, can I please ask you to read this paragraph 12 and to see what the security -- the command security organs, what their duties are, and what are their responsibilities in relation to their superior command.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security organs report to the superior military officers about their work and to the security organs of the superior command, to the units or to the staff, pursuant to the provisions of this rule. You will excuse me, because a little bit earlier I kind of went to the wrong side. Had somebody, before I came to testify, indicated anything like this, I would have gone to the military library in Belgrade, I would have taken these rules. I would have looked at them in a little bit more detail, and then, pursuant to my duties and my rank, I would have been able to be more precise, more specific. I must admit that I have forgotten the rules a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. I apologise. Well, if you can just tell the Trial Chamber, in relation to this paragraph 12, who was the superior officer in your corps and who were the security organs from the superior command? You can give us their names and their functions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My immediate superior to whom I reported and before whom I bore full responsibility, I was duty-bound to be neat and to also execute all my tasks professionally, that person was General Novica Simic, the commander of the East Bosnia Corps. As for the professional direction, it was the security organ in the superior command, and that was the chief of the Sector for Intelligence and Security Affairs in the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. As we can see -- I'm actually not going to deal with the rules anymore. Can we now, please, look at your statement which you provided to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number is 1D733.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is now P2183.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 17 of this statement, please, lines 10 through 22. Thank you. And in English, that will be on page 18. Thank you. The last paragraph in English. Thank you. Could we show -- have the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And I would like to ask you about the prison commander or warden, whose name was Djoko Pajic, as we can see in line 3 up here, and you described and talked about him. Now, my question is this: Whom did Djoko Pajic report to and whom did he have responsibility to report regarding his carrying out of his duties or tasks assigned? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djoko Pajic and another officer before him were directly responsible to the commander of the East Bosnia Corps, General Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And tell us, briefly, who was their immediate superior officer? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 18 of your statement, if we can pull it up, and that's 19 in English, or 20 in English, rather, here you say that this gentleman, Djoko Pajic, and you say that on line 31 and 32, he was the prison or camp warden, and he had within it a squad, a strengthened squad of policemen who were in charge of security. Now, who was this camp commander, as you mention here, and what -- where were these military policemen from, what unit were they from?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said in the interview, and I stand by that, the commander -- well, actually, I used the word "chief," and I believe that's how it was translated. But I don't think I said "chief" at the time. I think I used "warden" or "commander"; I'm not sure exactly what the title would be officially per establishment. But he was the responsible officer for this collection centre, whether he was commander or "komandir," and his name was Djoko Pajic. Now, before him, for a while, it was Gojko Cekic. So it is possible, theoretically, that in July and August of that year it was Gojko Cekic, but I'm rather inclined to believe that it was Djoko Pajic and that Gojko Cekic was already on some other assignment. And yesterday, in reply to a question by the Prosecutor about security, I said that the security and the guarding in the collection centre in Batkovic was provided by, as I said here, a strengthened squad. Basically, it would be the same thing, whether you said the strengthened squad or a platoon of some 20 to 25 men who were from a battalion of the military police of the East Bosnia Corps, and they were re-subordinated to the warden or commander of the collection centre. I'm not exactly sure whether he was defined as a warden or the commander per establishment. In other words, this strengthened squad, or weak platoon, was from the East Bosnia Corps Battalion, and it was re-subordinated to the warden of the collection centre in Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now see page 20 of your interview, lines 10 through 14.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, that's page 21, at the very bottom, and then it goes on to page 22. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The investigator, in the course of the interview, quoted General Simic's words, his testimony before this Tribunal, and he claimed that this is what was said, I quote: "... and then I ordered that the commander of this camp be arrested and that they be -- that the guards be suspended, that military policemen be deployed who had undergone the necessary training for this type of mission, guarding prisoners," and so on. And then he goes on and says -- well, I won't go there. So my question is this: In view of what General Simic said here, and as he testified in the Popovic case, and this was put to you by the investigator, did General Simic, when he arrived, did he actually remove the old commander and put in place this new commander, Djokic [as interpreted], in order to have the collection centre operated in keeping with the regulations and rules? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of this that General Simic testified about was something that happened before I was appointed chief of the intelligence and security organs in the East Bosnia Corps. I was briefed on this, and, among other things, General Simic also replaced the commander of the military police battalion. This is what he said here also in this portion of his statement. And he appointed Major Keserovic as the commander of the military police battalion. And later on, when the situation became more stable, Keserovic was promoted and assigned to a higher post, while Captain Vulin, later Major Vulin, was the acting warden, and that's the person that I found there when I got there. I also see that "Kizerovic" is mentioned here in this interview, but his name was actually Keserovic. S, yes, that's it. Now, the next step that was taken in order to improve the situation and make it function properly was to appoint a new commander or warden of the Batkovic Collection Centre. The man that General Simic mentioned, who had escaped or was banished from there, I didn't even know. Now, the military commander of the collection centre, Lieutenant-Colonel Gojko Cekic, that's the man that I knew, and then later on he moved on to another duty. And in his place a reserve officer was appointed by the name of Djoko Pajic. He was a prominent citizen in Bijeljina. Security in the collection centre was provided by the military police, or, rather, by this strengthened squad, or weaker platoon, some 20 to 25 military police, with their commander. And up until this centre was closed down, the commander/"komandir," was a man called Milenko Lujic. Now, when speaking about the way the work was done and conducted in the collection centre in Batkovic and how proper it was, from the time when I was appointed up until the moment when the collection centre was closed down, there were no deviations in the work. I would also like to note the following: Up until early 1994, or maybe even before the end of 1993, when I arrived in the corps command and became its member, I proposed to the commander that Lieutenant-Colonel Petar Jovanovic be transferred from -- who is now late, because he had a physical disability and he could not really be very effective in this job because that called for great physical acuity, that he be reassigned to some less-demanding duty in the corps command itself, at the headquarters. And in this conversation that I had with the corps commander, we came up with this idea that the corps commander should issue a decision and establish a garrison command which would then be in charge of garrison duties, including tenancy problems, health-related matters, military prisons, discipline and order, and so on, and that the said Lieutenant-Colonel Petar Jovanovic should be appointed to that duty. And that is what happened, so that the military prison was removed from the barracks, from the barracks compound, which was at the time in the offices of the military police battalion within the barracks compound, and the prison was then moved to Vanekov Mlin, to this other facility, and that's how it was known from there on. To provide security for this prison --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, I think you gave a very lengthy explanation with many details, but it was a very short and precise question by Mr. Tolimir. I think he should have the opportunity to move to the next question. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. You described now how order was re-established once Commander Simic arrived there. Now, please take a look at page 26 of your interview.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, that will be 28, page 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 26, lines 4 through 31, you describe that. Now, my question is this: Were all prisoners of war who were in Batkovic, who were inmates in the Batkovic Camp, had they all been registered by the International Committee of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I state this with full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, were all the prisoners held -- war prisoners held at Vanekov Mlin, were they all registered by the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that with any certainty, when speaking about this facility, because for a brief period in late July and early August, when prisoners of war were brought from the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps, now whether those prisoners of war were registered or not, I'm not sure. It is possible that they were only interviewed and then just records kept about them within the Drina Corps, itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We will ask you specifically about those prisoners that were referred to during the examination-in-chief. Now, the prisoners at Vanekov Mlin, were they registered and were their records kept within the military records or the military police records, the military police that were in charge of the camp?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, they were, because why -- if they hadn't been, why would then the warden, the prison warden, call me in the middle of the night and ask that I confirm that the said person was a member of the security organ and that I should talk to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I will now ask you about Avdo Palic, specifically. Was he registered by the guards at Vanekov Mlin, the military policemen who were there providing security, and was he in their records?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is the same as the previous one. I never had occasion to see that log, log-book, and say, yes, he was registered under number so and so. But based on everything I know, I would conclude that he must have been registered in that log-book, that it must have been registered that he had spent some time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is it because of that that the commander of the police security securing Vanekov Mlin, that he required that he could only be taken away once a form was signed? Does it also tell us something about the fact that they were registered?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This also indicates that Milan Savic - that was the name of the warden - was a responsible person, and in the log-book, where the name of Avdo Palic stood, he simply didn't wish to sign off that easily or leave empty the date of Palic's hand-over. He wanted to have him registered, and the warden wanted to have all of his bases covered once Palic was taken to another location.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. You noticed that the receipt was issued on the 5th, the receipt that was signed in Vanekov Mlin. It was issued by the Security Service there, confirming that the prisoner was handed over to the person in question.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the form, but I can't remember the date. I even remember the contents, but not the date itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Have a look at it in e-court. It was a Prosecution exhibit, I believe. Let me check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is P2182.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please have P2182, then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says the 5th of September, although the 9, standing for September, is not that clear. But I think it is 9, not 8. So the 5th of September, 1995. And in the text itself, I see again the 5th of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could the upper left-hand corner of the B/C/S document be blown up, please. Sir, now you can see a bit better, I think, the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is easier to read. We see that the figure 8 is of the same quality in both lines, but I believe it is a 9. Actually, the figure of 9, yes. We see the top of the number missing, whereas the bottom part of the number 9 looks like what it should look like. It's not an 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Given that there was disagreement between the commander who was in charge of the prisoner and the person who wanted to take him over, did the person who came to take the prisoner away have a written form, some type of confirmation that he is authorised to take him away?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him, and I didn't ask him whether he had such a form. I explained yesterday or the day before that I was called by Mr. Savic simply to verify whether Dragomir Pecanac was an authorised officer of the security organ of our superior command, and he also told me that he was refusing to sign off. However, since it is stated here that he was transferred following to the order of Tomic, Dragan, officer on duty of the Eastern Bosnian Corps intelligence organ, I suppose -- or, rather, I conclude that Dragan Tomic, as the officer on duty, called the officer on duty in the Intelligence Sector of the Main Staff in order to verify whether Pecanac was, indeed, there because of the needs of the service or of his own accord. So I believe he could testify to this. Perhaps Tomic and Savic provided their statements or testimony to the investigating judge of the BiH Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I will put some questions and you will have freedom to respond in the way you deem appropriate, but let's keep it short for now. We saw the date here, which is important, and it is the 9th. And since he did not have any written document with him and that you had to run your checks by phone, I wanted to ask you this: Do security organs need to know what tasks they are to go about when performing their duties?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will repeat. Since you said that the officer on duty had it confirmed by phone that -- whether Pecanac was, indeed, from the Administration Sector, my question is this: Do officers on duty in security organs and intelligence organs have to be acquainted of the tasks performed by other agents of the Security Service or do their chiefs have to be familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officers on duty, in principle, have to be acquainted with the situation and events preceding their shift as well as the most important tasks that will spill over into the next. All tasks received by individual members of the department, irrespective of the level, that is something that they need not be necessarily acquainted with, especially if these are counter-intelligence tasks or state security-related matters. In such instances, only the chief sending the person in question would be familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Since we saw that Mr. Beara issued a written order to Mr. Carkic, which you could read yesterday, dated the 10th of August, to bring Avdo Palic to Vanekov Mlin, do you think the competent officer should have also issued an order for Avdo Palic to be taken away from Vanekov Mlin, since this prisoner was, in a way, specific, unique?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In any case, he should have had a piece of paper authorising him to do this, because soldiers who are in military detention have a specific time to serve, say, between the 5th and the 15th, and on the 15th their commander comes and picks them up without a written document, because it had already been specified that they were to leave the unit on the 15th. But if we have this type of detention, when we know when the person came but don't know how long he will be staying, once that person is to be transferred, there must be or ought to be a document specifying the date, be it a telegram, a written order, some kind of document that would be used as the basis for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Having in mind that the person who came for Avdo Palic did not have a document authorising him to take him away and that this was done outside regular working hours and in an unspecified time, could it have been possible to conclude that he came there of his own accord to simply take the person away, which was further corroborated by the fact that he refused, initially, to sign that the prisoner was handed over to him?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak with certainty whether he did or did not have a document with him, but I infer he did not, since he refused to sign. His identity, though, was checked by the person on duty, through the administration, and I recognised his voice. The rest includes questions that should be put to him, if he's still alive and kicking.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 07321 for the witness. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You analysed this in detail yesterday, and you noticed an error in the date and the title. You can see that it was signed by Ljubisa Beara. Do you believe that a similar document should have existed on the taking over of the prisoner, because in this document he mentioned that it was essential that an interview be conducted with the prisoner?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, such or similar documents should have existed. However, in wartime conditions, frequently, because of the need to resolve matters quickly, such things could be also dealt with by phone, as long as they are noted down in the various work and log-books.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever discuss later on with the person who sent Mr. Palic to Vanekov Mlin about the fact that Avdo Palic was taken away in the manner he was?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never did. We never broached that topic. And I never met Avdo Palic. I didn't know what he looked like. When testifying before the BiH Court, I was shown a number of photographs and I wasn't able to identify anyone. I never discussed this topic with Mr. Beara, and we didn't talk much ever, because, being his subordinate, it wasn't up to me to put such questions to my superior, as you are well aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. A moment ago, we saw the rules and competences, and we could see that he was not your superior. He was actually someone from the superior command. He never received a written document on -- about the rather odd circumstances in which that prisoner was taken away, did he?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are different things that seem odd, as you put it, in the whole situation. Mr. Beara sent this document, which has almost nothing to do with the Security Service. It was a detention measure involving a person who was deemed important. We also discussed the issue of military detention, whereby we said that the military detention unit was a part and parcel of the garrison, with its own commanding officer, and everything that had to do with the military detention unit was dealt with through the garrison commander and the corps commander. Had it been mentioned in this document that me, as the chief of security of organ of the East Bosnian Corps, should undertake certain specific measures in order to protect this person, then it would have involved me directly. Absent that, it all has to do with the line of command which was supposed to receive that person, according to the rules, house him in detention, and document it appropriately, including his release or hand-over.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. I apologise if I said something or suggested something in my question which was inappropriate. I wanted to know, basically, whether the person who sent this document should have signed another document on the prisoner being taken away. I wanted to ask you this: Did the prison or detention commander, or Commander Simic, who was his superior, ever notify the Main Staff that the person was taken away from Vanekov Mlin by a certain person under rather strange circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've already answered. There should have been a similar document, documenting his release. But I did also stress that in exceptional circumstances, as envisaged by the Rules of Service, there may be occasions in which orders can be conveyed by phone, but then both persons at the different ends of the line have to have a document in their note-books and then it is of the same level as a document which would be sent in written form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You didn't understand the question of Mr. Tolimir, I think. He was asking you if the commander of the prison or Commander Simic ever sent a report to his superior Main Staff about the release of the hand-over of Avdo Palic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, during our daily briefing the following day at the office of the commander of the East Bosnia Corps, the garrison commander, Lieutenant-Colonel Jovanovic, Petar, reported to the corps commander about the procedure of the detainees being taken out from Vanek's Mill. I don't know if General Simic reported this further up to the Main Staff. I wasn't informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. My next question is this: Since this was not part of your responsibilities, you were there informally, but you did get some information about the activities --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure what the accused said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please repeat your question. It was not properly recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, since you just happened to learn that Mr. Avdo Palic was taken away from Vanek's Mill in odd circumstances, at night, without documents, did you perhaps ever speak about this matter with me, about the manner in which he was taken out? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I never asked you -- or I never talked about this topic to you. We didn't see each other too often, due to the circumstances which were what they were. I avoided asking any of my superiors questions, that included you, Beara, and others, all the more so because all the extremely professional, true officer relations with you, which I remember with affection, I asked you a couple of times about something, I asked after your health, and your answer was always pending. So I would always think carefully before asking anything of my superiors. I'm not really that curious by nature, generally, and I don't really ask many things that have not much to do with my direct responsibilities. These circumstances were odd. A person appeared from the administration, led by Mr. Beara. My duty operations officer checked. Somebody did respond and said, Yes, yes, Pecanac was sent. He called the warden of the detention unit, who was suspicious about the whole thing, and finally things culminated with me being woken up and this elderly man, the prison warden, said, I should ask Colonel Todorovic just in case. I do not want to be blamed for anything later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. I am obliged, for the sake of our professional relationship, to say that you did not have any opportunities for personal contacts with me, because I was in Dayton, after that I was in Vienna, I was away for a considerable period of time, and that is probably one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] now, can we please look at 65 ter 04086. So can we see 04086 in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I would like to ask the witness the following question: It was 1.00 in the night. You got the phone call, and you were told that Mr. Pecanac was there in the prison to take over Avdo Palic. Did you ask for any letter of authority that this Mr. Pecanac really had the right to take the prisoner away under these odd circumstances, as you called it? Did you ask for any document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't ask for any kind of permit, any document. The detention facility warden was acting pursuant to his rules and powers. His immediate superior is the garrison commander. He is the one who trained him and asks him to behave pursuant to the rules. And if there are any false steps or mis-steps, he would be subject to penalties. So I'm not sure whether he had any documents with him. If this is important, perhaps this is a topic for Mr. Simic -- I'm sorry, Mr. Savic, not Mr. Simic. I am thinking of Mr. Savic, who was the detention facility warden. I am not thinking about the corps commander in this case. The warden of the military detention facility called me on the telephone. This is a person who is about my age, and we knew each other privately; we were relatives. And because of this personal trust, he called me and he asked me, What should I do, Colonel? The matters stand like this; this is what it's about. And my duty officer also informed me that he had contacted the Security Administration at the Main Staff and that Pecanac, member of the Security Service, and he works -- this is something that I know, also Tomic knows it, who was the duty officer, that he worked at the Security Department. It does not have to be relevant. He was working today and perhaps this evening he could have been replaced and he could have escaped, deserted, and he could be presenting, introducing himself under a false function. Well, the matter of dispute was that should he sign it or not. The detention facility warden did not call me with the question, Do I have a document or not, or anything else. The only thing that he was concerned about was that he did not want to sign it. And I said to him, If you don't want to, then don't hand it over to him. And that's when Pecanac took the receiver, Why, how sign? I said, You sign pursuant to the protocol. Do not create problems for the detention facility warden. After that intervention, he did sign for him, and he took away the prisoner. I don't know what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, were you called that night because you were a relative of the warden or because of your position and your responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was more -- I was not the detention facility's warden superior officer along any command line. He had three -- or two or three other options open to him: to call the duty operations officer at the corps command, who was some 100 metres away, physically, he could consult this person; he had the duty officer at my sector, because in any kind of matters relating to the security officers they would call the Security Sector. He did call the Security Sector, and my duty officer said that Pecanac was the authorised senior officer from the security organ of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. There was a third option that he could have used along a private line, but not because I was his superior or because he was duty-bound to consult me, but it was some kind of human need and because of the trust he felt towards me. It was something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You said, on page 29, lines 19 and 20, and I quote: "My duty operations officer checked. Somebody did respond and said, Yes, yes, Pecanac was sent." Somebody did respond. Are you referring to a person in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, my duty operations officer dialed the duty officer at the Main Staff Security Administration. He introduced himself, and he opened -- he responded briefly, Yes, yes, Pecanac is responsible for that assignment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you give us the names of your duty operations officer and the person in the Main Staff whom he called that night? Do you recall the names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The certificate that we were able to see, it states that the duty officer of my sector, his chief was Dragan Tomic. He was a lawyer. I don't know who the duty officer was at the Security Administration of the Main Staff and who responded to his call. I don't know who was in Bijeljina and who was available and who was supposed to be consulted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was the duty officer -- your duty officer in the corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my duty officer was Lieutenant Dragan Tomic. At the Security Department, where I was the chief, the officer there was Dragan Tomic. He first got information or a request from the detention facility warden, who was checking whether this was an authorised person or not. My duty officer, Dragan Tomic, called the Security Administration of the Main Staff and asked whether Pecanac ... and so on and so forth. And when that didn't work, then they called me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you very much. We must have our first break now, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we see 65 ter, on the e-court, 04086. This is a document by the Main Staff, Sector for Intelligence/Security Affairs, and this document concerns the peace negotiations in Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are you aware when the Dayton talks took place and when the peace agreement was signed?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. Even without looking at the document, I know that the Dayton final document was signed on the 21st of November, because, again, this is linked with one of our Orthodox holidays. I can see that the negotiations were conducted from the 1st to the 21st of November, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Then during that period of time, as indicated in the document, from the 1st to the 21st, was I able to be in touch with you for you to be able to let me know any information about the activities that we have been discussing earlier? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, physically, a body cannot be in two places at the same time. And before this 1st of November, you were appointed, I assume, to be a member of the commission or the team, and I assume that you had duties of such a nature that you needed to prepare. So I guess you had fewer opportunities for any kind of contacts, including those with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please tender the document, since it also covers the period when I was abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was I present during the period when Mr. Pecanac turned up to take Mr. Palic out of Bijeljina? Was I present?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a specific answer to that question because I don't have a record, not even a record of my movements during those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. In the first line of this, it says: "In the period of the 1st to the 22nd November, 1995, at the American base Wright-Patterson in Dayton, peace negotiations were held ..." Look at that. And now can you please look at the ninth paragraph: "A delegation of Republika Srpska was led by ..." And then it says, further down, the delegation also included Zdravko Tolimir, General, and so on and so forth. Is that the period during which this activity took place when the prisoner was taken out from Vanek's Mlin? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a little bit later than the period when Avdo Palic was taken away. But one could conclude that you were obliged, much earlier before this time, to gather materials to compare, to compile documents. I assume that you were busy in the delegation, performing certain assignments and tasks, so I assume that you were absent. But I don't really have any kind of record of your working time to know when you were at your post and not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Earlier, you looked at this certificate, and you even remarked that it was drafted in September and not in August. We're now going to show P2182 in the e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And before that, can we admit the document that we are looking at in e-court right now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is quite difficult -- No, please, back to the previous document. It is quite difficult for us to understand what we see on the screen, because you didn't put questions to this document to the witness, Mr. Tolimir. We don't know anything about this document. We see a date, the 25th of November, 1995, and it's obviously from the Main Staff of the VRS. But what is it about? You should use this document with the witness. And I would like to see the last page to see who signed it. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I signed this document, and I asked the witness if he could see, on the first line of this document, when the Dayton negotiations took place. And he said that he knew the date without even having to refer to the document. And can we now show the first page, please. Then I asked him to look at paragraph 8. Can we scroll up so that we can look at paragraph 9, actually, to see who comprised the delegation of Republika Srpska. Can we now look at the heading, about which -- actually, in this paragraph, it says that in the delegation, besides other members, Zdravko Tolimir was also a member. And now we can look at the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And you can tell us, Mr. Todorovic, whether you ever received this report from Dayton. Was it ever sent to you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to answer your question, I did receive this report. I recall it very clearly. And in reply to your previous question, I said that you could not be in two places at the same time, both in Bijeljina and in the Main Staff, because at the time you were in Dayton as a member of the delegation of Republika Srpska, and that was between the 1st and the 21st of November. Now, I also said the following: that before November the 1st, when you were in Dayton already, you probably had to take some time to prepare for that major task, meaning the work that you had to do as a member of the delegation, which would mean probably that you had to be busy with that for about a month. Now -- and then that brings us to September. Now, when exactly in September you were there, I can't really say exactly. But from this document we can see, and I understand, that you must have had some time that you needed to prepare for this delegation, and that you were probably absent from your duties and that somebody else was standing in for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This document --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Wait a moment, please. This document will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 4086 shall be assigned Exhibit D223, marked for identification, pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now Judge Mindua has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not really a question; it's just a point of clarification. Since the document is not translated: Who is the addressee of this document, please, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can see the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This was a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did see the last page of this document. The document was sent to all chiefs of intelligence and security departments within the VRS who were connected to the intelligence and security organ in the Main Staff of the VRS, to the commander of the main -- the chief of the Main Staff of the VRS, and the commanders and units that served within the Main Staff Command, and it was sent to all the commanders of units of the VRS in order to inform them on the outcome of the negotiations in Dayton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in your capacity as chief of the organ of the Security and Intelligence Services of the Eastern Bosnian Corps, that you received a copy of this document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, but not the chief of sector, but at the corps level, that is, the Department for Information and Security. Now, a sector is a superior institution that was at the level of the military staff, and that's correct, because on the last page you can see, at the bottom in Serbian, that this document was sent to the commanders, among others, my own commander, and security and intelligence organs or departments of my corps and all the other corps in the VRS, as well as to the Ministry of Defence and so on; in other words, to all the different levels and structures within the VRS, to the commanders and security and intelligence chiefs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, allow me to go back in time a little. I'd like to go back to a question that was addressed right before the break, and, unfortunately, I did not have time to address it then. Here we see that when an important issue is raised, the chief of the security and intelligence services can inform his subordinates about a particular issue. But how is it, then, that you, in the middle of the night, at 1.00 in the morning, you are woken up because a very important war prisoner is there, and he's referred to under a code-name, which is "Atlantis," this person is leaving the centre without a document and you don't inform your superior of the Intelligence and Security Sector about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've explained that, and perhaps there was an omission in interpretation or a misinterpretation. My duty officer, not my own personal, but, rather, the duty officer at the Intelligence and Security Department of the East Bosnia Corps, checked with the Sector for Intelligence and Security, or, rather, the Intelligence and Security Administration of the Main Corps of the VRS -- of the VRS Main Staff, whether, indeed, Major Pecanac was assigned this mission and whether he was sent to do this. And, practically, all the official -- all the things that had to be done officially had been exhausted thereby, and no one should have really made that phone call to me in the middle of the night for this reason. However, as I explained a little earlier, the prison warden, who was a personal acquaintance, and I've explained this as well, wanted just to double-check to make sure that there would be no consequences for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to tender this document, the document we have before us, unless it's already been done. And I would also like to call another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was marked for identification already.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm sorry, I failed to notice that. Could we have 05484 under 65 ter, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, the document that we see here on the overall Dayton Accords, negotiations and the accords and annexes, has this document been sent to you? Can you please take a look and check that, whether it was sent to the chief of the Security and Intelligence Department.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was sent to me as well, and I kept this document for a long time with me as a token of the sort of -- something to have a memento of the end of the war and the negotiations, so I kept it very carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you receive all the documents that were part of the peace agreement, and were they also sent to the security organs in units that were subordinated to you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were sent. Namely, in addition to this original document, there were also supplements to this, so that each unit and command within the corps had a set of documents with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now pull up -- or, rather, could we scroll this document in order to be able to see the note or comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And can you tell us whether this comment states precisely what you've just described here, that these documents are to be forwarded to all the subordinated security and intelligence organs within your units -- within your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I answered your question already. I anticipated, as it were, your question. And as I said, I kept this document myself, and all the units received them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you tell me now: After the signing of this peace agreement, was part of it the implementation of this agreement on the ground, and was it binding on the parties -- or, rather, the warring parties on the ground? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the focus and the main task for every unit. There were tasks that had to be implemented immediately, such as cease-fire and cessation of hostilities, and then there were tasks that were staggered, a 15-day, a 30-day mark, a 45-day mark, withdrawal, and so on. But the focus of all the work, the focus was on the implementation of the provisions of this agreement, and that was the focal point and the focal mission of all the departments for -- of the various security and intelligence departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we please see the last page of the document in both languages. I mean the page with the signature. I don't know which page it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's on the second page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I see it now. This document will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 5484 shall be assigned Exhibit D224. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now pull up 65 ter 05484. My apologies, my apologies. We've just seen that document. Can we see 05835. Thank you. For the record, let me say that this is a Main Staff document, dated the 7th of January, 1995, entitled "Meeting of the Joint Central Commission: Report."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question for you is this: Did you receive this document as the chief of the Security and Intelligence Department of the East Bosnia Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did receive it, and we can see that this document was sent, in addition to commanders who were related to the Main Staff. We see the 1st, 2nd, and so on, East Bosnia Corps. It was also sent to the chiefs of security and intelligence departments of those commands in order for them to be informed at the same time of the contents so that they can implement the tasks assigned therein as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, looking at this document, can you tell us whether this Joint Central Commission was the main body in charge of implementing the Dayton Accords?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 2 of this document, please. Paragraph 3, let's take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Above number 3, we see that it says: "At the fourth session of the Joint Central Commission, observation posts are to be agreed." And then it goes on to say: "The Commission also adopted the Agreement on the Cessation of Hostilities." That's on page 3. My apologies. I called for page 2. My question is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I'm not sure if we have the right document on the screen, or the right part of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 6 reads as follows: "The agreement was signed by Major General Manojlo Milovanovic, General Vere, and Colonel Stjepan Siber." In other words, the agreement referred to there is the agreement on the cessation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could the B/C/S version be enlarged, please. Do you see the relevant part, not above number 3, but below number 3, the next paragraph below number 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it, and I did notice it earlier as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And now your question, please, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: At every session of the Joint Commission which was held in Sarajevo under the auspices of UNPROFOR, were there specifically-assigned tasks and was there agreement on how to go about implementing those tasks, as established by the UNPROFOR commander and as assigned by the UNPROFOR commander?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After each of the meetings, we, the subordinates from the security organs, were informed about what was agreed upon, and we received specific orders as to how to proceed within our respective areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the corps, at its level, also have a central joint commission with the adjacent corps of the opposing warring sides, and were they in standing contact with that corps' commander?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Such commissions were formed at corps command levels, and they established direct co-operation with the enemy side. In my area, for example, it was with the 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of course through the mediation of IFOR, which was later renamed UNPROFOR. Shortly thereafter, although I don't recall the date, a meeting was held of those commissions at the highest level at the separation line, at Porebrice. Alongside the corps delegations, there were the commanders of the East Bosnian Corps, General Simic; and commander of the 2nd Corps of the ABiH, General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I note that this document and the previous one were not included in the list of documents to be used during your cross-examination. This is always unfortunate if it's not included. Perhaps we have received, in the meantime, another version, but my last one didn't include that. The document will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 5835 shall be assigned Exhibit D225. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D719, or P1011, because the latter has a better translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, do you recognise the document, and what does it pertain to? Also, was it forwarded to your corps as a document on the completion -- cessation of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with the document. It is one of a number of documents which appeared during combat activities, which lasted for a short while only, after which immediately combat was resumed. This is the 23rd of December, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: During this cessation of hostilities, were there any violations along the front-lines concerning a number of soldiers that were supposed to be exchanged between the VRS and the ABiH? And when I say the "soldiers," I have in mind the soldiers of your corps.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain that this agreement was violated. I'm trying to rewind. Sometime around that date, there weren't only violations but also breakthroughs through the front-lines and taking soldiers captive, although I can't recall anything specifically. All I can say, that basically this agreement never even lived to see it become true.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go to the last page to see who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It was signed by both political and military leaders. Was this agreement signed by the Croatian military and civilian leadership?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the left-hand side, we can see "Alija Izetbegovic" and "Rasim Delic," who was commander of the Main Staff of the ABiH, then "Kresimir Zubak," who was the political representative in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who was a Croat. And "Vladimir Soljic," I don't know that person by name. I can't say what his ethnicity was. On the right-hand side, we have "Radovan Karadzic," who was the RS president, and "Ratko Mladic," commander of the Main Staff of the VRS. At the bottom, we have the peace representatives, "Yasushi Akashi," from the UN, and "Sir Michael Rose," who was at the helm of the peacekeeping force.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
