utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether absent from this document are the signatures of the commanders of Croatian ethnicity, Croatian armed forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I tried to comment what positions were that these people held. It was only Rasim Delic, who was from the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Ratko Mladic, who was from the Main Staff of the VRS; these are the only two military representatives. The other people we see here were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I apologise for repeating my question, but I have to do it for the record. Was the document signed by the commander of the HVO in Bosnia and Herzegovina; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did UNPROFOR tolerate the fact that the Croats did not sign the agreement for as long as they had an opportunity to deal with some things they wanted to see resolved by military means?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned of that through official information, about this kind of conduct or position towards the different warring parties. Personally, I never attended such gatherings, but I was informed of it through official channels, not from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Following the signing of this Agreement on the Cessation of Hostilities, was there another outbreak of conflict in the RS and the Serb Republic of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could conclude that more intensive preparations began for the final stages or operations of driving rebel forces out of Croatia. I had it confirmed through intelligence information we had. The Republic of Croatia was bringing in and grouping, as well as training and equipping, the units of their army alongside selected routes, and their focus was Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you recall when Croatia drove the Serbs of the Serb Republic of the Krajina out, thus eliminating the RSK as a protected UN area?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The beginning of that operation was in early August. I don't know if it was the 2nd, the 3rd, or the 5th of August, 1995. The operation itself did not take long.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether NATO, too, participated in the bombing of Serb positions attacked by the Croatian Army and ABiH in the western part of the SRK [as interpreted] and the RS, where units of the 1st Krajina Corps of the RS were located?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It should have been "RSK" instead of "SRK."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the few days following the exodus of the population from the RSK, I went to Drvar on official business, and I could see a location that was hit by aeroplanes. A refugee column was targeted, and one could see things strewn about and traces of bombing. I don't know what plane -- or what force that plane belonged to. Because it was outside the area of my corps, I couldn't identify the plane itself. I don't know whether it was an Italian plane, a Croatian plane, a NATO plane. I don't think, though, that Croatia at the time had its own aviation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Tell us this: Based on this agreement and the joint operation between the HVO, the Croatian Army, and NATO, can we make any inference as to why they didn't sign this Agreement on the Cessation of Hostilities at that time and for what reason?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a military point of view, there is something worth taking note of. The so-called corridor in the RS was a route through the Brcko area. At that time, it was under threat, and the forces defending it were disproportionately low. The East Bosnian Corps, upon orders of the Main Staff, we were obliged to send assistance to the Krajina Corps. We supplied a number of units. Not a single bullet was fired along the corridor during the operation when the RSK was liberated and the population driven out. The reason for it was that the population had to be allowed to go through the area without any hindrance. At that point in time, the corridor could have been cut in half by, let's say, a reinforced battalion or a unit of similar size. However, it did not take place. This makes me conclude that it was a planned and carefully-organised operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Did NATO bomb exclusively the western part of the RS around Banja Luka in the areas of the 1st and 2nd Corps, and they did not bomb the area of your corps, where the corridor was used by the Serbs fleeing Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document, Mr. President. Oh, it has been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, we saw a number of documents testifying to my absence, because I was busy with other tasks related to the Dayton Accords. Let us again look at P2182, again. Perhaps now, following that document, you will be able to say where I was at the time all this was happening, because previously you said you couldn't confirm that. We see here the receipt of the 9th of September -- actually, the 5th of September, issued by the authorities in the prison about the handing over of Avdo Palic at Vanekov Mlin. Since the date is the 5th of September, and following all the documents we saw, can you recall whether I was in the RS or abroad?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can repeat that I can only presume. I cannot state with full responsibility that you were absent between the 3rd of -- that you were absent at the time because of the Dayton Accords and that in your absence your assistants stood in, who were in charge of intelligence and security. However, I cannot be more concrete than that, and I cannot specify a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we've seen in the Dayton Agreement document that on the 1st of September I was in Dayton, until the 21st -- actually, from the 1st until the 21st of November, could you please tell us, for the purposes of the transcript, could I have been both in Republika Srpska and in Dayton from the 1st to the 21st of November? Actually, could the transcript reflect correctly your answer, since you already gave an answer. So could the transcript correctly reflect whether you said yes or no. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is that you could not have been in Republika Srpska or in the Main Staff, performing your duty by establishment. Also, I can state with full responsibility that for a considerable amount of time before that period you had to have been absent from your duties in order to adequately prepare for such a complex and big assignment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, I would like to ask you: Have you any knowledge where Mr. Tolimir was on the 5th of September, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know anything about the 5th, 6th, or the 20th. It wasn't his duty to report to me or it wasn't my duty to report to him on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just wanted to know if you have any knowledge where Mr. Tolimir was on that day, 5th of September, 1995. I'm putting this to you because Mr. Tolimir asked you several times about November and the Dayton negotiations. But this document we have on the screen is dated on the 5th of September, 1995. Do you know where Mr. Tolimir was at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, can we now look at page 42 of your statement, please, to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is P2183, P2183.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we ask e-court, please, to show P2183.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 43 in the English. We are interested in lines 17 to 22 on this page 42. I am going to read to you. During the interview, the investigator asked you this: "Do you have an explanation why -- do you know of any reason to divert thousands of prisoners of war from Batkovic, instead of back to Batkovic, and housing them in little schools around the Zvornik area? Do you have any explanation why --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just wanted to know where you are -- this portion is to be found, but now I see it. Lines 27 and the following. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And the investigator then asks you: "Do you have any explanation why that would have been done to thousands of prisoners?" And then on line 27, you said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note we do not have the text on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we don't see the next question of the investigator. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm sorry to interrupt, but General Tolimir keeps referring to this question as one that was put to this witness. It wasn't. He's reading from a transcript that was put to a different person, and so the questions and the answers relating to that person is what is being put to this witness. So I just wanted the record to be clear about that. The question is actually put to Ljubomir Mitrovic in the Popovic case. So we see the questions that were put to him and the answers that he gave, and then this witness was asked to comment on it on the next page. But I just thought that should be clear for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please take that into account.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Can we now look at page 44 in the English and page 43 in the Serbian, lines 5, 6, and 7. What Mr. Vanderpuye has said is exactly right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You answered: "There's no logical explanation, both from the point of view of an officer, of a soldier, a human point of view, or morale, or ethics. The only explanation can come from the point of view of a mentally unbalanced person who could think of something like that, which is something that I'm deeply ashamed of." Thank you, and I have now ended quoting.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the page that you were reading from is not shown to me on my monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the e-court please show that page to Mr. Todorovic so that he could see what I asked him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, yes, I see it now. Yes, yes, this is what I said, because we were talking about what happened after the fall of Srebrenica, or, rather, when Ljubo Mitrovic explained that they did not come to Batkovic at all, that their visit was cancelled, and that on the route from Srebrenica to Bijeljina they were deployed at a number of locations along that road. And the epilogue of all of that is known to everyone here. And my answer was as it is stated in the document, and I stand by that same answer now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Since you've already answered my question in part, I'm going to just ask you this: When you were giving your statement, were you questioned about your knowledge about why the order was changed to send the prisoners of war to the Batkovic Camp? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, there was a question like that. You'll remind me if I've forgotten. My answer was that to this day I still don't know who made that decision, why the decision was changed. I didn't really look into this. It's something that I never looked into professionally or privately. I never showed any interest in learning who made this decision and acted in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at D3, please. This is a statement by General Major Elliott, who was the -- who was Carl Bildt's secretary. In paragraphs 2 and 3, he talks about how, on the 14th and the 15th, General Ratko Mladic was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you know that Ratko Mladic was absent at that time and that he was in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know -- from the media, I know that when Srebrenica was de-blocked and liberated, he was in Srebrenica. The footage of that is being played over and over again in different media outlets. I don't know whether this was the 14th or something. Immediately after that, he went to Belgrade. This is something that I also knew from the media, that he went for some kind of consultation or agreements or talks. I don't know of what nature. I assume that it was about the newly-created situation and further actions. I didn't attend the meeting, so I'm only assuming that that was what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. We can see what the documents say about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D655 or D192, page 6, last paragraph, paragraph 17. This is a statement, as you can see, given by General Rupert Smith to the Dutch NIOD, the Dutch institute that was investigating the Srebrenica events. Can we look at paragraph 17 now, please. And if we can look at the last paragraph, which is on page 6 in the Serbian version, and this is already shown in the English version, paragraph 17, which is above, immediately above, paragraph 18. We need to look at that part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And it states -- I quote what Mr. Rupert Smith said: "Eventually, Mladic gave permission to the ICRC to visit the prisoners. At that time, he was not concerned about reports that the BSA had separated men and women in Srebrenica, as the ABiH did exactly the same when they captured large villages." Did you know, through the media or in other ways, that General Ratko Mladic approved or allowed the ICRC to register all the prisoners of war in Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know from the media, as I said, from the footage that is constantly being played, and from looking at parts of the transport of the population from Srebrenica to the B&H Federation, that the buses and the trucks that were going mostly were transporting women. There was the odd man, also, among them. As for the records and the presence of certain institutions, I really couldn't say anything about that as precisely as I have been able to talk about matters in the East Bosnia Corps AOR. That was my responsibility. You could see in the footage also vehicles of the then UNPROFOR and other international institutions. I assume that they did compile some kind of record. I don't know whether they did manage to compile complete records or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at D193 now, please. This is a statement by General Rupert Smith that he gave to this Court on the 14th of August, 1996. Yes, thank you. Can we ask the e-court, after showing the first page, to show us page 17, paragraph 4. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see the first paragraph in English. That is what we will be looking at. And we can see the last paragraph on that page in the Serbian version, where General Smith states on the first line that General Mladic was in Belgrade on the 14th of July for meetings. And then in line 5, he states that he was also there on the 15th of July. And then in line 11, he says that Milosevic imposed on Mladic to allow access of humanitarian agencies to Srebrenica and to permit freedom of movement for UNPROFOR and UNHCR, and so on and so forth. I would like to ask you this: Did you also perhaps hear through the media anything of what was at the meeting that was held between General Milosevic, General De Lapresle, Mladic, Rupert Smith, and others who were present at -- in this delegation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned a little bit earlier that I assume and believe, as an officer of my rank, that that was the course of the conversation or the talks in Belgrade. All the more so because after the meeting the Republic of Serbia organised a reception centre for Muslims who had crossed over across the Drina in the broader area of Uzice. I assume that during the talks an agreement was reached with General Mladic to provide transport and the possibility to relocate those who wanted to go to Tuzla, or Sarajevo, or anywhere they decided in order to resolve the situation of a large number of people in one place in circumstances that were very difficult for survival.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at D152. Can we not, please, broadcast the document publicly because this is a statement by Witness PW-06, who's protected. Can we look at page 3 in the Serbian, paragraph 1, and page 3 in the English, also paragraph 1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And we can see where it states -- in the first line, you cannot see the whole sentence. It says: "... a jeep arrived, and he was in uniform. I knew it was Mladic, as I recognised him, and I was told that he would come. I was about 10 to 15 metres from him when he gave a speech, standing by the side of the pitch. He spoke without a megaphone, just normally, as it was very quiet. He stated that he was General Mladic and said that we would all be exchanged and that there were hundreds of Serb lines between here and Tuzla and that not even a bird would be able to get through the lines. He said we would be organised into groups to collect all the bodies from the hills and then we would be taken to Bratunac to have lunch there. He then chose five of his men to begin making lists of our first and last names, which lasted nearly an hour." And so on and so forth, end of quote. Now, did you see, in the footage showing General Mladic during those events, General Mladic addressing the prisoners and saying that they would be exchanged? These were the activities that took place on the 13th. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could not have been the 13th. He was in Belgrade on the 13th and the 14th. Perhaps it was the 12th. I did watch the footage repeatedly, a number of times, of his address, and, in a way, I saw the expressions of gratitude on the faces of those present, in a way; also about the words he had directed at the persons who were present there who I could see in the footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the topic also discussed here during this case was the fact that somebody had changed the decision about sending the prisoners to Batkovic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my testimony, from the beginning of the interview with me in Belgrade, and then on Monday when I was questioned by the Prosecutor, up until now, I keep saying, and I responsibly stand by that, that the command of the East Bosnia Corps received a telegram informing us to make preparations for whatever this -- the name of this general was who wrote this document that I'm looking at in front of me now. I don't know why somebody changed this decision which had been issued at that time. I don't know that to this day. In your conversation -- I mean, in my conversation on the telephone with you, it was evident that they were not coming. And then General Simic, my commander, ordered that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. We will deal with that later, but let's just stay, so that we maintain continuity, let's stay with this.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the participants of those -- a participant in those events, during trial here, Captain Nikolic, on page 60 of the transcript, lines 15 to 16, stated that Colonel Beara, on the 6th of April, at a meeting held at the SDS, told Deronjic that he had an order from his boss that everyone should stay in Bratunac? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm not sure if we have a -- well, I think -- I'm quite confident we have a translation issue. What we have in the transcript here is: "... that Colonel Beara, on the 6th of April, had a meeting at the SDS, told Deronjic that he had an order from his boss that everyone should stay in Bratunac." It just seems to be completely in contradiction to the evidence in the case, so I thought we should straighten that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, I was surprised about that as well. Please check what you were talking about, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Perhaps I was speaking too fast, perhaps unclearly, so we will clarify that now. Page 12420, lines 9 to 16, Mr. Nikolic states: "Then, at the meeting, everybody thought they should be killed in Bratunac." It says "everybody thought," and not "everybody said." "At the beginning, Colonel Beara was the one who insisted that they need to stay in Bratunac, regardless of the fact that I was already travelling to Zvornik to convey the order. I don't know exactly what happened, but I can assume that probably in the meantime, in all that confusion, there was a change in the order. But I don't know that. I cannot talk about that because I don't know whom they received the order from. I am just saying what I know." End of quote of what Witness Nikolic stated, who was an eye-witness and who was present at the meeting that was held at the SDS premises in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So my question is this: Since Mr. Nikolic also said there was a change of order involved, did the Prosecutor, when he questioned you, when he talked about a change in order, did he tell you anything about a change of the order, since you gave your own comment on that and in view of the fact that only somebody who is not quite in their right mind could do something like that? So were you told anything else? Do you know any other details about this change of order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just ask General Tolimir to clarify that question. It's, first, a bit long, and, secondly, it talks about changes in an order which he hasn't identified for this witness. One is a change in order that Nikolic, the witness, testified about, which is a separate issue altogether than what this witness has testified about in his direct examination and so far on cross-examination. So to the extent that there's a change in the plan or a change in the order, it would be helpful if General Tolimir could clarify specifically what he's talking about and put his case to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I asked the witness whether he had been shown a portion of the testimony in the Popovic case, where those things were said about the prisoners of war, and he gave his answer. So that is the basis for my question. That was number 1. Number 2, I also read out a portion of what Nikolic had said about the change of the orders, and I said, When Nikolic said at the very beginning Colonel Beara was the person who insisted that they should stay in Bratunac, irrespective of the fact that I had already gone to Zvornik in order to relay that order. In other words, he went to Zvornik to tell them that they would come to Zvornik, and then suddenly there was a change in orders. And then he goes on to say, I don't know exactly what happened, but it's possible that in all the confusion that ensued there was a change in the orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So my question is this: From what Mr. Nikolic said, is it clear that there was some kind of change in the orders that were issued that he knew nothing about? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to put this question in a different way. Do you know anything about the change of the order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't really know. And that's what I said earlier. What I do know is there were orders to make the preparations. And since that did not happen, I then called and asked, When are they arriving? And then they said, You can stop with your preparations; there was a change. And why this happened, I don't know, and I haven't found out to this day. And I think there was a slight error in the transcript. The date that is mentioned for the meeting was the 5th of April, but that's impossible because -- because the 5th of April and July are two completely different months. So it's impossible that this meeting would have been on the 5th of April with Beara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know if this was just a slip of the tongue or a misinterpretation - probably a slip of the tongue - but Mr. Nikolic was the one who testified on the 6th of April in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's correct. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to belabour the point. It's just that the meeting itself is recorded as having occurred on the 6th of April, which is not possible. So I would appreciate it if that's clarified for the record so that we know what meeting we're talking about and when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which meeting are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm referring to the meeting that was held on the 13th, going on the 14th, the SDS session, the meeting that was attended by Beara, Deronjic, and Vasic, and that was the meeting that Mr. Nikolic referred to on the 6th of April of this year in this case before the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you mean the 13th and 14th of July, 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. Thank you, Your Honour. My apologies. I omitted the month and the year. This was on the 13th, going on the 14th of July, 1995. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, do you know anything about this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know anything about this meeting then or later, much later. I only learned later on by watching some TV programmes which showed footage of some Parliament sessions. And among other things -- or, rather, court sessions, court proceedings. And among other things, I happened to watch a report from the court where this was mentioned. So I didn't have any information on that meeting then about the meeting itself. And what I learned later on from various sources, that was really not my personal knowledge, and I can't really say anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, your next question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, in order for us to be able to focus on the questions, and I notice that you wanted to discuss this issue of when the prisoners of war would arrive at your site, and I would now like to show document P2183, page 32 in Serbian and 35 in English, lines 25 through 34. This is the first draft or the first version of what you said about your contacts with me, and then we'll see that later on that changed slightly in answer to various questions. Now, you say the following, and I'll quote: "I cannot be sure about the dates --" "I cannot be sure about the dates, but I will tell you what I was tasked to do in relation to that. Whether this happened in direct contact with him," and you're referring to me there, "or by telegram that we received, it's very difficult for me to say after all this time has elapsed." Based on what I've read out, my question is this: Can you tell us now whether this happened in direct contact or whether you received a telegram? Regardless of how that can be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we see here before us, that's correct, that's what I said. This was the first interview with me, and I said that in answer to questions about the events that were far later, and that is why I said what I said there. After this, I gave this some thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. I'll put some additional questions about this. So you say -- you go on to say the following: "I was supposed to convey to the commander for him to take measures that Batkovic be prepared -- that hangars be prepared for accommodating 1200 people who had been captured in Srebrenica, and that they would be brought to Batkovic." Thank you. So my question is this -- we'll come to my next question later, so my question relating to this is the following: From what you say here, is it clear that General Simic, as the commander, was supposed to take steps to prepare Batkovic for accommodating a certain number of prisoners of war? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During this interview with the investigator, I used civilian terminology, more or less, and that is why I used the phrases "to take steps" or "to request" or "ask him," "to convey that to him," and so on; however, now, as I sit here today, as a witness and as an officer, in military parlance that would mean that I would have to convey an order from a superior command, in other words, from the Main Staff, to him, and that he should, as a commander, take steps to make preparations for the accommodation and reception of this number of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. Could you tell us now: Did I have the right to issue orders to corps commanders, and was that within my ambit and within my competencies? Could you tell us, under the law, how was that, and what is your opinion of that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could not issue orders to corps commanders or to any other commanders from subordinated units. You could convey an order from the commander of the Main Staff, but then you would have to indicate, "by authority of," so and so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's take a look at the last two sentences in this paragraph: "In a way, we were fortunate, in this unfortunate affair, because we had some 40 people who were captured, members of the VRS, who had been captured in Majevica and who were in Tuzla, and once these prisoners from Srebrenica arrived, we figured that we would be able to exchange them for our own men." Thank you. End of quote. So my question is: Were you happy about suggestions or proposals such as these, or were you happy or fortunate because --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter requests that the question be repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The end of your question was not interpreted to us and not recorded, Mr. Tolimir. Please repeat the last -- just the last part. The beginning of your question was: "Were you happy about suggestions or proposals such as these ..." And you should continue again your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So was it our good fortune, relating to these proposals or suggestions that were made, of course, pursuant to an order that you said had not been sent to you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said this in the statement. This was a stroke of good luck and this whole misfortune, misfortune because there was this huge number of prisoners of war and because of their suffering; that was the misfortune. The good stroke of fortune was that we would in this way be able to exchange our own men for these members of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we need our second break now. Could you tell us the time you need for concluding your cross-examination after the break? I expressed my expectation to be able to finish with this witness today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think we will be able to complete our questioning if the witness sticks to the questions and gives brief answers, without giving his own broad descriptions. I think we can actually complete it today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means you need the remainder of the hearing today. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. As I understood, your prior direction is that your expectation was that the witness's testimony would be completed today. In view of the detail to which -- into which his cross-examination has gone, I don't anticipate being able to complete his -- a redirect examination, which I think may be necessary, within the amount of time we have left, even assuming that General Tolimir hurries through the remainder of his cross-examination. I just don't think that it's possible to finish it. And I understand your direction, and I hope to abide by it, but I just want to let you know that it's really not quite that possible at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Indeed, under these circumstances, it's not possible to finish with the witness today. Mr. Tolimir, you have used five hours and nine minutes up to now. We have our second break now and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. We stopped at page 33 in the Serbian, lines 17 through 19. That is page 35 in the English version. You say -- I hope you can see the line on the screen. It is where the cursor is: "I can't recall the date. I don't know if it was on the 12th, 13th, or the 11th, in the evening, but immediately following the fall of Srebrenica. It was definitely not on the 15th." Next, in line 24 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we need the English text on the screen as well. Could you say on which page we can find it? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 35, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Next, in lines 23 through 27, which is the next page in the English, you say that you do not exclude the possibility that we either met or that a telegram arrived. Based on that, I wanted to ask you the following: When providing this interview, did you always repeatedly say that you were uncertain about the time, precisely, because a lot of time has elapsed, and that you cannot be specific as to the date?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is there a possibility that later on, when questions were put to you and insistence placed on confirming something you cannot recall, you made certain changes to the original interview you provided in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially, yes. But the gist of my original statement remains unchanged.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at page 37 in the Serbian, lines 21 and 22, and then 27 through 34. Page 39 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In line 15, you were asked this: "Do you remember what date that was? Approximately." And you respond: "Between the 15th and the 20th of July." In line 27, you say: "I don't recall exactly what the date was, and I don't know whether it was in person or by telegram," when Tolimir told you to prepare Batkovic. So in line 32, you said that you couldn't be specific on that either.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is what you recall accurately reflected in the interview you gave in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just a brief remark, though. I think that the 15th or the 20th has to do with the other piece of information and that is that all preparations were to be stopped because they weren't going to arrive at Batkovici. It didn't concern their reception.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you remember what happened between the 15th and the 20th at Baljkovica or in the AOR of the Zvornik Brigade through which the Muslim division was breaking through?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning the dates following the 12th of July, in the AOR of the Zvornik Brigade, there was combat. There were attempts for columns of soldiers and civilians from Srebrenica to forcefully break through to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well see D176 in e-court, page 4, please. Thank you. We see it now. Please turn the next page - my mistake - which is page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On this page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which page in English ?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Four -- sorry, 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The - first, second, third, fifth - sixth bullet point, where it says: "The 2nd Corps Command." It says: "In the morning on the 15th of July, 1995," it is page 6 in English, "in the general area of Snagovo, significant combat could be heard. We learned that parts of the 28th Land Force's Division were engaging in combat, and in their reports they refer to us as the aggressor." Were the media also reporting on conflicts between the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina's forces breaking out from Srebrenica and the forces of the Zvornik Brigade at Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see this document for the first time. I can't comment. As for the media, yes, they were reporting on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you see that on the 15th the breakthrough began, and does this tally with what you recall of those events?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can see from the document that on the 15th these things transpired. As for what I said in my interview, mentioning the 15th or the 20th, this was an approximation which I gave after quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The information that was made public through the media, was it the basis for the conversation you and I had over the phone, which you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next please have 07314. 07314. We can see it in the Serbian. Can we have it in English as well. It's an order of the Main Staff of the 16th of July, sent to the Command of the East Bosnian Corps, the Drina Corps, the 1st Light Podrinje Brigade, and the Zvornik Brigade. We see that it has to do with a transfer of detainees to the Batkovic Camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the introduction, it says: "Based on demonstrated need and for the purpose of the more effective exchange of detainees, I hereby order:" Can you tell us whether the demonstrated need pertained to the prisoners of your corps, and was their exchange something that was expected?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank God that finally I can see the document we have been discussing all along. I've been trying to say that there must have been a document issued to the Command of the Eastern Bosnia Corps when it was ordered to receive prisoners from the area of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see, in item 1, the following: "Transfer all soldiers and civilians who are now in the prisons in your zone of responsibility to the Batkovic Collection Camp in Bijeljina." Is this camp -- was this camp under your corps control?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at item 2: "In its zone of responsibility, the Command of the Drina Corps and the Eastern Bosnia Corps shall organise the transport of detainees to the Batkovic Camp in Bijeljina." My question is this: Did they, indeed, bring in those detainees, apart from the ones you brought in from Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No prisoners were brought in before there was a final agreement between General Simic, commander of the East Bosnia Corps, and Colonel Pandurevic, which was after the 15th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I have to interrupt for a moment. I see in the head of this letter the date of the 16th of July, 1993. And you see, under item 4, that: "The Command and the DK shall report to me ... no later than 22nd of July, 1993." I don't know if this is just a typo or an error. I have no idea. But it seems to be a document from 1993. Please clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It says "1993," as you specified. I wanted to ask Todorovic this:

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The other document, in terms of order format, was it similar to the one we are looking at now?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't even notice the date. I was so happy to see this; that's why I said, "thank God." It was something similar that arrived on the 11th, 12th, or the 13th, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you please explain why you said "thank God." What was it what you wanted to express?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to express the following: All along, from the Belgrade interview until this moment, I was asked and expected to be precise and specific in terms of dates, document contents, and who wrote what, who it was sent to, et cetera. However, when I saw this, I thought it was the document from 1995, and I was happy to see that there was something concrete that finally I wouldn't have to guess on as to whether I have to provide an answer about the 11th, the 12th, or the 15th, because I really can't recall the date and specific detail. Time has taken its toll. And when I saw this document, I was relieved of this burden, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand. But now you see this is a document with a date of 1993. Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I wasn't in the East Bosnian Corps on that date. This is July, and I only joined the corps in November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. My question is this: The order you saw a moment ago, was it similar, in terms of format and content, to this one from 1993, given that the Prosecution doesn't have that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think that the order is of similar format and content and that it arrived, but it had the number 1000 -- 1200, the approximate number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 02264. This is a 65 ter document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please look at the fifth paragraph. And before that, I'm going to say to the transcript that this is a document of the 26th of July, 1995. Paragraph 5, beginning with the words: "On ..." and this is the second paragraph up from paragraph marked "2." This is in the English, and it states: "Thirty-four straggling enemy soldiers from Srebrenica surrendered in the course of the day. They were taken to the prison in Batkovic." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does this report indicate that some order was sent according to which the prisoners from the corps were supposed to be taken to Batkovici, because this is a document dated the 26th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the contingent that was handed over and taken to Batkovic on the basis of agreement of the commander of the East Bosnian Corps, General Simic, with Colonel Pandurevic, the commander of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But here, there is 34 and 26 mentioned. In the other one, it was the 16th, in your statement about combat and the conversation between Simic and Pandurevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then and now, I would like to keep emphasizing that I cannot remember the date. It's been a long time since then. I don't know if this was on the 15th or the 16th. Here, we have 34 in total because during the combat and the surrender of those who were trying to break through towards Tuzla in combat, they were taken to the Batkovic Collection Centre. Actually, approximately 160 to 180 prisoners of war were taken to the Batkovic Prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic. I'm just looking for things that are going to help you remember and also help us to present to the Trial Chamber all the relevant facts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this document that we're looking at now so that I could call up another document into e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we please clarify, before that, what is your intention in relation to 65 ter 7314. That was the document of the 16th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise. Could we tender this so that we could see who was responsible for ordering units in the Army of Republika Srpska to transfer prisoners from one zone to another. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7314 shall be assigned Exhibit D226.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And 65 ter document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, wait a moment. We have still on the screen 65 ter 2264; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Indeed, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I didn't see the signature. I would like to see that first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document will be received as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2264 shall be assigned Exhibit D227.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, since this is a document dated the 26th of July and it was signed by the commander of the Drina Corps, does that mean that there has to be an order ordering him to send all the prisoners from his AOR to the East Bosnia Corps AOR, and does all this indicate that you actually did see an order to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 02688, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can I ask you now to look at the contents of this order, signed by the justice minister, Zoran Cvetanovic [phoen]. And it states: "In reference to your memo," number such and such," please be informed that in memo 04/1/9-85 from the General Staff on the 7th of March, 2001, we subsequently received --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't know why I don't know this document. We have to clarify that before you are continuing reading into the transcript. It was a prosecution document, I was told.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Probably because of the names, because there are lists inside. So probably it's under seal because of the names of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Anyway, my question to the witness is this: Does this document provide information on the prisoners being sent to the Batkovic Prison after the events in Srebrenica in July?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I would also need to see the attachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please ask the e-court to show the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We're not broadcasting this document, I take it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. The reason for it is because of the names on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And these are in the attachment, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: They are in the attachment; that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. You may go to the next page without broadcasting it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see a list here. Can you please look at the entries. The dates, all the dates, are later than the 18th of July, meaning that this is after the events in Srebrenica, after the breakthrough. The list has the names of -- and we will look at the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we turn a few pages so that we can see that the list contains 171 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You will see that for yourself. And the remark also notes that the listed persons are also registered on the list of the ICRC, and the ICRC representatives were present during their exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Only a minor point. General Tolimir's question is translated as his having said that the dates are later than the 18th, and I think you can see in e-court, on the first page, at least, that there are at least five on the first page and a few also on the third page, and so on. So the record should just reflect that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we go back to the first page of this list. And now to the next page. Thank you. There are some entries of the 18th of July, 1995, but not before that. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, there are entries on the 18th on the second -- that's the first page here that I see in e-court, and then there are entries on the 18th, skipping a page after that, and then there are entries on the 18th again, skipping a page after that. So it would be pages 1, 3, 5, and 6, it looks like, and 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, did all of these exchanges take place after July 1995 - thank you - as it states in the heading of the document that the exchange was effected at the end of the year?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is clear and confirms the number that I gave as being between 170 and 180. The list contains the names of 171 persons. I assume, since this is easier for me to decipher, and I don't want to mislead anyone, I think there is a typo. The person under number 1 entered Batkovici on the 18th of July ... May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And they left the 10th of July, so this is not logical. They cannot be released before they were admitted. So this is probably the 10th of September. That should probably be the correct date. Or perhaps the 10th of August. Perhaps we need to go through the whole list, because the exchanges were effected on different dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. That is very helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's one thing that doesn't make sense. It's probably a typo. Perhaps the list needs to be checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, when you looked at the list and you spotted the errors that you drew the Chamber's attention to, and when -- these persons who were exchanged from Batkovici after the events in Srebrenica, did they come to Batkovici after the events in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were they all registered with the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that is what it states in the note on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were they there, all of them, from the 18th to the 23rd, the 24th, the 25th, the 26th? Is that the date when they entered Batkovici, and later they were exchanged, and is this something that you can see from this list? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. May I, briefly, just for a minute, so that I confirm the things that I have been saying so far. And that is that the military police unit that was going to the Zvornik Brigade AOR on a daily basis from the 18th up until the 26th, depending on the number of prisoners that they were taking into custody every day, they would bring them in, accommodate them, and register them at the Batkovic Collection Centre. So it does not stand, what was said in one of the statements that I saw here, that a military police platoon of the East Bosnia Corps took part in combat actions, because a part of the military police unit from the East Bosnia Corps went only when there was a certain number of prisoners of war captured. They would take custody of them and escort them to the Batkovic Collection Centre. And so I have been repeating that since Belgrade up until this point in time; I've been repeating that constantly. And now I can really stand by the dates, even though I don't have my work note-book or any kind of work document. And I would like you to understand that it's very difficult for me to say whether something occurred on a very specific date or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, are you aware that the corridor for all Muslims who were trying to get through from Baljkovica was open with the agreement of the Zvornik Brigade commander, and that is the route used by those who were breaking out through from Srebrenica and going towards Zvornik and Kladovo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It states "Kladovo." Actually, it's not Kladovo; it's Kladanj. Kladovo is in a different state. Actually, I didn't know that at the time because I was busy with my own assignments. Later, I learned about that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Todorovic, did you have chemical devices in order to suppress demonstrations in the police units of the Eastern Bosnia Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, and I think I do know, we didn't have such equipment or devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The units in which you served, did they have such devices or equipment at their disposal? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that they had such chemical combat devices in their depots and at their disposal. But during our training, we did study that form of combat means and their applications. As a person who went to the Staff School, I did put the question whether I or any of my colleagues would need to have such devices, and the answer was, If there is a need, then we would have such devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at P2155, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what about the document we just had on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, Mr. President. I would like to tender it and have it admitted, if possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received, under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2688 shall be assigned Exhibit D228, to remain under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, you can see here that the command of the 27th Logistics Base, for the needs of the Drina Corps, on the 21st of July, forwarded, one, chemical rifle grenades, SKD M-83, then chemical rifle grenades SKE M-83 and special hand-grenades, M-79 AG1. As a soldier, can you tell us what this "M-83" and "M-79" stands for?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When there is designation "M" on lethal assets, it means that it was the year when the prototype, with the production of the assets, was initiated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at D200 next, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you please repeat the number of the document we have just seen because the number was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, a moment ago we saw P2155.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we are looking at D200.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, you can see before you a rifle grenade. It is M-83 we saw a moment ago on the document. It's a chemical rifle brigade [as interpreted] for training purposes, M-83. The title was not translated. But how can you tell that this is a training asset, rather than a lethal asset?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All assets, such as ammunition, mines, et cetera, that are used for training soldiers and officers were marked in yellow, including the text, so as to distinguish it for security purposes, so that in the course of training, true lethal assets would not be used by mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we next see D201. And this has already been admitted, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see here a special hand-grenade, M-79 AG1, the same one referred to in the previous document. Do you recognise it as a training asset?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same answer applies. We can see the red line.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Yellow line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: During your education, were you told that it was made available to units of the military police in order to suppress riots and control masses?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This type of asset was at the disposal of the civilian and military police. They were mild tear gas assets causing temporary inability to act and not causing death or injury. They were usually used to suppress riots. This is not a chemical weapon belonging to a category of weapons of mass destruction.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We did our best to conclude with your testimony. I have no further questions of the witness. I wish him a safe journey back and a happy life in retirement. Thank you, Mr. Todorovic, and greetings to your family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have to adjourn for the day. We are at the end of today's hearing. We resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom, Courtroom II, and then Mr. Vanderpuye, for the Prosecution, has some additional questions for you. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 21st day of April, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
